title: Human Resource Management Essentials
summary: Learn the core of HR: recruitment and selection, onboarding and training, performance management with SMART goals, pay and employee relations, wellbeing, diversity and HR metrics.
audience: Students, new managers, small-business owners and people starting HR careers

body.p: Human resource management (HRM) is how an organisation attracts, develops, rewards and keeps the people it needs, while treating them fairly and within the law. In a small business the owner does HR; large organisations have HR teams and specialists, but every manager still makes daily people decisions.

list: Workforce planning: how many people, with what skills, when.
Recruitment and selection: finding and choosing employees.
Onboarding, training and development.
Performance management: goals, feedback and reviews.
Pay, benefits and recognition.
Employee relations, health and safety, discipline and grievances.
Records, HR data and compliance with labour law.

body.p: Good HR supports the organisation's strategy. A firm planning to open three new branches needs to recruit and train managers months in advance; a firm moving online needs digital skills. HR turns these plans into people plans.

body.tip: Labour laws differ by country (for example South Africa's Labour Relations and Basic Conditions of Employment Acts, Nigeria's Labour Act and Kenya's Employment Act). Always check the rules that apply where you work.

body.p: Recruitment attracts suitable applicants; selection chooses the best of them. Start with a job analysis: what the job involves (the job description) and what the person needs (the person specification: qualifications, skills, experience and attributes).

list: Internal adverts reward existing staff and are cheaper.
External channels: job boards, social media, universities, agencies and referrals.
Write clear, inclusive adverts with the real requirements, pay range and how to apply.
Avoid requirements that unfairly exclude groups, such as unnecessary age limits.

body.p: Use the same structured interview questions and scoring guide for every candidate, linked to the person specification. Skills tests and work samples often predict performance better than unstructured chats. Check references and qualifications, and record why decisions were made.

Measure the process: if a firm spends R60 000 on adverts, agency fees and interview time to make 4 hires, its cost per hire is 60 000 / 4 = R15 000. Time to fill and new-hire retention are other useful measures.

body.tip: Ask behavioural questions such as "Tell me about a time you handled an angry customer"; past behaviour is a good guide to future behaviour.

body.p: Onboarding helps new employees become productive and feel they belong. People decide early whether to stay, so the first weeks matter. A good programme covers the paperwork, the workplace and tools, the culture and values, and clear early goals, with a named buddy or mentor.

list: Identify needs by comparing required skills with current skills (a training needs analysis).
Choose methods: on-the-job coaching, job rotation, workshops, e-learning, mentoring.
Evaluate: did people learn, did their behaviour change at work, and did results improve?
Plan careers: show staff how they can grow, which helps retention.

body.p: Training is an investment. If staff turnover falls because people see a future in the firm, the savings in recruitment and lost productivity can far exceed the training cost.

body.tip: Ask new hires after 30 and 90 days what helped and what was missing, and improve the programme from their answers.

body.p: Performance management aligns each person's work with the organisation's goals and helps them improve. It is a continuous cycle: plan goals, support and give feedback, review, and reward or develop.

list: Specific: clear about what is to be done.
Measurable: you can tell whether it was achieved.
Achievable: realistic with the resources available.
Relevant: linked to team and organisational goals.
Time-bound: with a deadline.

body.p: "Improve customer service" is vague. "Answer 90% of customer emails within 24 hours by the end of June" is SMART.

Give feedback often, not only once a year. Describe the specific behaviour and its effect, and agree on next steps. In reviews, use evidence, avoid bias (such as judging a whole year on one recent event), and separate development conversations from pay decisions where possible. Poor performance should be addressed early and fairly, with support and a clear improvement plan.

body.tip: Ask employees to assess themselves first; it makes reviews a conversation rather than a verdict.

body.p: Reward includes basic pay, overtime, bonuses, benefits (leave, medical aid, pension, transport) and non-financial rewards such as recognition and flexible work. Pay should be fair inside the organisation and competitive with the market, and must at least meet any legal minimum wage.

If an employee earns R50 an hour for a 45-hour week and works 5 extra hours paid at 1.5 times the normal rate, weekly pay = 45 x 50 + 5 x 50 x 1.5 = 2250 + 375 = R2625. The legal overtime rate and maximum hours depend on the country and contract.

list: Give every employee a written contract or statement of terms.
Have clear policies for leave, conduct, grievances and discipline.
Discipline must be fair: investigate, let the employee respond, act consistently and keep records.
Dismissal needs a fair reason and a fair procedure, or it may be challenged at a labour court or tribunal.
Respect workers' rights to join trade unions and bargain collectively.

body.tip: Most disputes start as small misunderstandings. A quick, private conversation often solves what a formal process would escalate.

lessons.title: Health, wellbeing, diversity and HR data

body.p: Employers must provide a safe workplace: assess risks, train staff, supply protective equipment and report serious incidents. Wellbeing goes further: reasonable workloads, support for mental health, and preventing harassment and bullying.

Fair treatment regardless of race, gender, disability, religion, age and other protected characteristics is both a legal duty in many countries and good for performance. Practical steps include structured hiring, fair pay reviews, reasonable accommodations for disability and clear anti-harassment policies.

list: Staff turnover = leavers / average headcount x 100. With 18 leavers and an average of 120 staff, turnover = 15%.
Average headcount: starting the year with 100 and ending with 140 gives (100 + 140) / 2 = 120.
Absence rate = days lost / days available x 100. 240 days lost out of 120 staff x 220 working days is about 0.91%.
Also track time to hire, training hours and engagement survey scores.

body.p: HR data includes sensitive personal information, so store it securely, limit access and follow data-protection laws such as POPIA, the Nigeria Data Protection Act and Kenya's Data Protection Act.

body.tip: Hold exit interviews; patterns in why people leave point to the fixes that matter most.
